topic: The Early Stuarts & the Origins of the Civil War 1603-1660
subject: history

items.title: Charles I lost the Civil War partly because he was a poor commander
items.claim: What contributed to Charles I's defeat (1642-1646) beyond political 'tyranny'?

options.text: Parliamentary forces always vastly outnumbered the king's

Parliament held London (wealth, manpower), the navy, and after 1645 the New Model Army; Charles repeatedly failed to coordinate his commanders and missed strategic opportunities like marching on London after Edgehill
The Scots refused to fight on either side
Charles was killed in battle at Naseby

items.reveal_title: The man, not just the cause
items.reveal:
After the indecisive Edgehill (October 1642), Charles failed to march on London while it was undefended. The Solemn League and Covenant (1643) brought Scottish forces in on Parliament's side. The New Model Army (formed 1645) under Fairfax and Cromwell was the first national professional army.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646; they handed him to Parliament. His attempts to negotiate while plotting a second war (the 'Engagement' with the Scots, 1647) destroyed any remaining trust and led to his trial.
items.why: Wars are won by armies, logistics and leadership — not just by who has the better political argument. Charles's strategic failures are often glossed over in the rush to debate 'tyranny vs liberty'.

items.title: The Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961) was a CIA-trained failure
items.claim: What happened at the Bay of Pigs?

options.text: A successful US Marine landing in Cuba

Around 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles (Brigade 2506) landed at Bahía de Cochinos on 17 April 1961; without expected US air support, they were defeated within three days, with 114 killed and around 1,200 captured
A peaceful protest broken up by Castro's police

items.reveal:
The operation was planned under Eisenhower and inherited by Kennedy after his January 1961 inauguration. Kennedy cancelled the second air strike that would have neutralised Cuban air power. The exiles landed in swampy terrain with no popular uprising materialising.

Kennedy publicly accepted responsibility — 'success has many fathers, failure is an orphan' — and the CIA director Allen Dulles resigned. The prisoners were exchanged in December 1962 for $53 million of food and medicine.

The humiliation pushed Castro further toward the Soviet Union; Khrushchev's decision to place missiles in Cuba in 1962 followed directly. Operation Mongoose continued covert efforts against Castro through the 1960s.
items.why: Failed interventions can be more consequential than successful ones. The Bay of Pigs led directly to the Cuban Missile Crisis — and reshaped Cold War risk-taking for both sides.
